body: {"total":8,"records":[{"title":"Assumptions and biases of the test-negative design for influenza vaccine effectiveness: a methods overview","authors":"Lindqvist-Obuya H, Moreau-Santos C, Tanaka-Pearce D","year":2016,"venue":"Epidemiologic Methods Review","doi":"10.5555/emr.2016.0081","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We describe the assumptions under which the test-negative design gives unbiased estimates of influenza vaccine effectiveness. The key assumptions are that vaccination does not change the risk of illness from other causes, that vaccinated and unvaccinated patients seek care alike, and that testing does not depend on vaccination status. Biases arise from broad or inconsistent case definitions, late specimen collection, inclusion of repeat tests from the same patient and poor adjustment for calendar time. We recommend that studies report each of these choices explicitly."},{"title":"Methods reporting in 112 test-negative influenza vaccine effectiveness studies: a systematic survey","authors":"Achterberg-Mbeki T, Castillo-Rhodes J","year":2019,"venue":"Journal of Vaccine Epidemiology","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We systematically surveyed 112 test-negative studies of seasonal influenza vaccine effectiveness published between 2010 and 2018. Only 38 of 112 studies restricted testing to patients meeting a clinical case definition. In all, 44 percent adjusted for calendar time at intervals finer than a month, and specimen timing after symptom onset was reported in 61 percent. Prior-season vaccination was measured in 27 percent. Reporting was most complete in studies from established sentinel networks. The authors propose a minimum reporting list for future studies."},{"title":"Repeated testing and prior-season vaccination in test-negative studies: a simulation study","authors":"Okafor-Lindholm P, Varga-Nakamura E","year":2021,"venue":"Epidemiologic Methods Review","doi":"10.5555/emr.2021.0144","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We simulated test-negative studies under realistic testing patterns to examine two common choices. Including repeat tests from the same patient biased estimates towards the null by up to 8 percentage points when testing was frequent among vaccinated patients. Ignoring prior-season vaccination distorted estimates when repeated vaccination changed the protection given by the current vaccine. Restricting to the first test per patient per season removed most of the bias from repeat testing. The simulations assumed accurate laboratory tests. The authors recommend that every study report both choices explicitly."},{"title":"SARS-CoV-2-positive controls in test-negative influenza vaccine effectiveness studies after 2020: a methodological review","authors":"Harrington-Adeyemi S, Kowalczyk-Moyo R, Ito-Brennan F","year":2023,"venue":"Journal of Vaccine Epidemiology","doi":"10.5555/jve.2023.0209","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed test-negative influenza vaccine effectiveness studies published since 2021 for how they handled patients who tested positive for SARS-CoV-2. Of 46 studies published since 2021, 29 excluded SARS-CoV-2-positive patients from the control group, 11 kept them and 6 did not report the choice. Keeping them as controls can bias estimates when COVID-19 vaccination is correlated with influenza vaccination. Few studies reported sensitivity analyses for this choice. Studies that kept SARS-CoV-2-positive controls came more often from settings with high COVID-19 vaccine uptake. The authors recommend reporting results both with and without them."},{"title":"Rapid antigen versus PCR testing and outcome misclassification in test-negative influenza studies","authors":"Duarte-Whitlock M, Sorensen-Obi A","year":2024,"venue":"Clinical Virology Methods","doi":"10.5555/cvm.2024.0117","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared rapid antigen tests with PCR in 2,860 patients with influenza-like illness who were tested with both methods in sentinel practices. In all, 21 percent of rapid-antigen-negative patients were PCR-positive, so rapid testing would place many true cases among the controls. In a simulated test-negative analysis, relying on rapid antigen results alone lowered vaccine effectiveness estimates by 9 percentage points. Misclassification was greatest early in the illness. The authors recommend confirming negative rapid tests by PCR in effectiveness studies."},{"title":"Register-based versus self-reported vaccination status in test-negative studies of older adults","authors":"Petrakis-Grant L, Mensah-Holloway J","year":2018,"venue":"Vaccine Research Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared self-reported influenza vaccination with the immunisation register for 1,530 adults aged 65 or over enrolled in a test-negative study. Self-report agreed with the register for 86 percent of participants. Disagreement was more common among people with cognitive impairment and among those vaccinated in pharmacies, whose vaccinations were sometimes missing from the register. Effectiveness estimates differed by 5 percentage points depending on the source used. The authors recommend linking to registers where possible and checking pharmacy records for people vaccinated outside general practice."},{"title":"Test-negative studies in care home residents: a scoping note on methods and gaps","authors":"Regional Vaccine Evaluation Group","year":null,"venue":"Public health technical notes","providerType":"report","abstract":"This technical note summarises how test-negative studies have included residents of care homes. It finds that residents are often excluded because testing practices differ from those in the community, that outbreak testing breaks the assumption that testing does not depend on vaccination status, and that very few studies report results for residents separately. The note gives no publication date and does not describe how studies were found. It recommends separate analyses for residents where numbers allow. Residents were included in fewer than one in ten of the studies it describes."},{"title":"Time since symptom onset and influenza vaccine effectiveness estimates: a pooled analysis of five seasons","authors":"Nyberg-Oduya K, Farrell-Tanaka S, Lopez-Achebe M","year":2022,"venue":"Journal of Vaccine Epidemiology","doi":"10.5555/jve.2022.0063","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We pooled five seasons of sentinel test-negative data to examine specimen timing. Estimates were 12 percentage points lower when specimens collected more than 7 days after symptom onset were included, because viral shedding declines and late cases are misclassified as negatives. Restricting to specimens taken within 4 days of onset gave the most stable estimates across seasons. Timing was missing for 9 percent of specimens. The authors recommend that studies report specimen timing and restrict or stratify by it. The effect of timing was similar across age groups."}]}
